title: Emotions as judgments
hookLine: Stoics saw destructive passions as mistaken judgments, not feeling itself

cards: Your friend doesn't text back. An hour. Three hours.
By evening you're sure: they're annoyed with you, maybe finished with you. Your stomach is tight. Then the phone buzzes.
Sorry, phone died, what's up? The whole storm is gone in a second. Nothing changed in the world.
Only the story you were telling yourself changed. The Stoics built a whole theory of emotion on moments like that one.

teach.b: Pathos is Greek, from a verb meaning to suffer, to undergo, to have something happen to you. English keeps it in pathetic and sympathy, and usually translates the Stoic word as passion.
For the Stoics, a pathos was a passion in a narrow sense: a feeling that runs away with you, that you undergo instead of choose.

They named four families: distress, fear, craving, and a kind of giddy, overexcited pleasure. Here's the surprising claim. Chrysippus, an early Stoic teacher, taught that these passions are judgments.
Not the cause of a judgment, not a side effect.
Inside every runaway feeling is a belief: something terrible has happened, or something terrible is coming, or I must have that, or this is the best thing ever.
And the Stoics said the belief is often false, or at least much too big.
Epictetus says it plainly in his Handbook, in George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Chrysippus had a picture for it.
When you walk, you can stop whenever you want. When you run downhill, your legs carry you past the point where you meant to stop.
A passion is running downhill. What the Stoics did not say: that all feeling is a mistake, or that you should become a stone. On the last day of this week you'll meet the good feelings they kept.
What they said is that the destructive ones carry a hidden sentence. Find the sentence and you can check it.
So the question that matters: what am I telling myself?

how: Stoic practitioners, and modern cognitive therapies influenced by them, look for the belief inside a strong emotion and ask whether it is accurate.

games.q: your friend hasn't texted back in hours, and you're sure they're angry. what would Epictetus look at first?
games.why: people are disturbed not by what happens but by their opinions about it. the silence was a dead battery.

practice: Bring up one feeling from today, even a small one: irritation, worry, wanting. Listen underneath it for the sentence, which usually starts with they, or I, or this: they don't respect me, I'm going to fail, this has to go well.
Hold it up to the light. Is it true? Is it the whole truth?

wordCard.voice: Pathos. Greek for something you undergo: for the Stoics, a runaway passion built on a mistaken judgment. Today's word.
